draft.title: Perfect squares and difference of two squares
card: Squaring a binomial gives \((a + b)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}\). The middle term is twice the product of the two terms, so it is not left out.
A sum times a difference gives \((a + b)(a - b) = a^{2} - b^{2}\). The two middle terms cancel, so only a square minus a square is left.

\(x^{2} - 49\) is a square minus a square, so it factorises as \((x + 7)(x - 7)\). \(x^{2} - 6x + 9\) has first and last terms that are squares and a middle term of \(-2 \times x \times 3\), so it is \((x - 3)^{2}\).
draft.remember: Squaring a binomial has a middle term of twice the product. A sum times a difference has no middle term.

a.why: Twice the product of \(x\) and 4 is \(8x\), and \(4^{2} = 16\), so the result is \(x^{2} + 8x + 16\). The option \(x^{2} + 16\) is the tempting mistake of squaring each term and leaving out the middle term.
a.clue: Write the middle term as twice the product of the two terms.

b.q: Which is the factorised form of \(9x^{2} - 25\)?
b.why: \(9x^{2} = (3x)^{2}\) and \(25 = 5^{2}\), so this is a square minus a square: \((3x + 5)(3x - 5)\). The option \((3x - 5)^{2}\) is tempting, but it expands to \(9x^{2} - 30x + 25\), which has a middle term.
b.clue: Find the square root of each term, including the 9 in front of \(x^{2}\).
